payload.abstract_signature: Optimal multi-agent performance is determined by the semantic coherence and interaction dynamics between agents rather than the aggregate individual benchmark scores of the constituent models.
payload.argument: Optimal multi-agent performance is determined by the semantic coherence and interaction dynamics between agents rather than the aggregate individual benchmark scores of the constituent models.
payload.canonical_key: optimal multi agent performance is determined by semantic coherence and interaction dynamics between agents rather than aggregate individual benchmark scores of constituent models
payload.discussion: The principle implies that quality control for autonomous coding agents should prioritize measuring dyadic or group interaction metrics (e.g., agreement rates, constructive critique frequency) over static capability assessments. In large-scale repositories, this suggests a calibration strategy where agents are paired based on historical interaction success rates rather than assigning the 'best' available model to every subtask. A limitation is that high coherence might sometimes indicate echo chambers rather than robust error checking, necessitating diversity constraints within the detected communities to ensure critical evaluation capabilities are retained.
payload.evidence: The work demonstrates that naively assembling high-performing models can stifle cognitive diversity and degrade collective output, whereas teams formed via interaction-centric graph clustering outperform random baselines and match manually curated teams. The evidence rests on the observation that pairwise conversation coherence predicts downstream collaborative success better than individual model rankings, validating that synergy is an emergent property of interaction rather than a sum of parts.
payload.name: Behavioral Compatibility Over Individual Competence
payload.problem_pressure: How can we provide real-time, calibrated, actionable process quality control for autonomous coding agents operating on large-scale repositories?

work_version_records.abstract: While a multi-agent approach based on large language models (LLMs) represents a promising strategy to surpass the capabilities of single models, its success is critically dependent on synergistic team composition. However, forming optimal teams is a significant challenge, as the inherent opacity of most models obscures the internal characteristics necessary for effective collaboration. In this paper, we propose an interaction-centric framework for automatic team composition that does not require any prior knowledge including their internal architectures, training data, or task performances. Our method constructs a "language model graph" that maps relationships between models from the semantic coherence of pairwise conversations, and then applies community detection to identify synergistic model clusters. Our experiments with diverse LLMs demonstrate that the proposed method discovers functionally coherent groups that reflect their latent specializations. Priming conversations with specific topics identified synergistic teams which outperform random baselines on downstream benchmarks and achieve comparable accuracy to that of manually-curated teams based on known model specializations. Our findings provide a new basis for the automated design of collaborative multi-agent LLM teams.
